claims.text: Under sustained loading, deformation in high-entropy-alloy multilayers is governed by the interplay of dislocation nucleation, dislocation motion, and lattice distortion.
Compositional complexity can be controlled to optimize deformation behavior.
Lattice misfit can be controlled to optimize deformation behavior.
Short-range order can be controlled to optimize deformation behavior.
The proposed starting materials are nanoscale high-entropy-alloy multilayers with varying compositional complexity and lattice misfit.
Lattice distortion caused by chemically diverse atomic constituents slows dislocation activity in high-entropy alloys.
Severe lattice distortion promotes dislocation nucleation while impeding long-range dislocation glide.
Increasing compositional complexity can replace planar slip and abrupt stress drops with more homogeneous flow and smoother serrations.
Short-range order can increase the force required for dislocation nucleation and increase dislocation pinning.
The proposed control strategy will enhance deformation tolerance relative to conventional metallic multilayers.
The proposed control strategy will enhance strength relative to conventional metallic multilayers.
Compositional complexity and lattice distortion can produce unusual deformation behavior.
Nanoindentation and microcompression can be used to examine deformation and dislocation evolution while compositional complexity and lattice misfit are varied.
Failure to observe any influence of dislocation nucleation, dislocation motion, or lattice distortion on deformation behavior would falsify the hypothesis.
